about.title: Rancho Cordova Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Rancho Cordova sits east of Sacramento along Folsom Boulevard, home to just over 71,000 people who rely on local clinics, urgent care, and hospitals across Sacramento County. Most visits go the way they should. When one doesn't — a missed diagnosis, a medication mix-up, a surgery that went off course — the questions can pile up fast. Was this an unavoidable complication, or did someone fall below the standard of care? California's MICRA law draws that line carefully. A poor result by itself is not malpractice; you generally need a qualified medical expert to show what a careful provider would have done differently. Timing matters too. You typically have one year from when you discovered the harm, and never more than three years from the injury, plus a 90-day notice to the provider before a lawsuit is filed. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect Rancho Cordova residents with an independent attorney who handles medical negligence cases on contingency, so there is no fee unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was hurt in a crash on Sunrise Boulevard and my treatment made things worse. Is that malpractice?
items.answer: Possibly, but it depends on the details. Rancho Cordova recorded 426 people injured in traffic collisions in 2025, and some of those patients later question the care they received. A crash injury claim and a medical negligence claim are separate matters with different rules, and an attorney can review whether a provider's decisions, not just the original injury, caused additional harm.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover in a California malpractice case?
items.answer: MICRA places a cap on non-economic damages such as pain and suffering, and that cap rises each year under current law. Economic losses like medical bills and lost wages are treated differently. An independent attorney can explain how the current figures apply to your situation.

items.question: My surgery didn't turn out the way I hoped. Do I have a case?
items.answer: Not necessarily. Under California law, a disappointing or even serious outcome is not malpractice by itself. The question is whether the provider fell below what a reasonably careful professional would have done, which usually requires a qualified medical expert to assess. Sharing your records with an attorney is the practical first step.
